questions.stem: A client agrees to receive care by telehealth. Which statement about informed consent is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Telehealth can have informed-consent requirements, and the clinician should follow applicable state law and document required consent for the virtual visit.","B":"Informed consent never applies to telehealth because no in-person examination occurs.","C":"Telehealth consent requirements are identical in every U.S. state and never vary by jurisdiction.","D":"Only the client has responsibilities in the consent process; the clinician does not need to explain what to expect from telehealth."}}
questions.rationale: HHS telehealth guidance states that official informed consent may be required and that specific consent laws vary by state. Clinicians should explain what patients can expect, address rights and privacy considerations, and ensure required consent is received and documented. The prior item was too broad in implying one universal telemedicine-consent rule.
questions.source_detail: Current federal telehealth guidance: specific informed-consent laws vary by state; explain what to expect and patient rights; receive and document required written, electronic, or verbal consent as applicable.

questions.stem: A nurse is repeatedly scheduled for prolonged work hours because of chronic staffing shortages. Which patient-safety concern is most supported by current ANA guidance?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Fatigue from long hours, heavy workload, and inadequate staffing can increase medical-error risk and requires both organizational and individual mitigation.","B":"Fatigue is only a personal wellness issue and has no meaningful relationship to patient safety.","C":"Mandatory or extended overtime is the preferred long-term substitute for adequate staffing.","D":"A fatigued nurse should never communicate concerns because staffing decisions are unrelated to professional safety responsibilities."}}
questions.rationale: ANA's position statement effective May 27, 2026 identifies nurse fatigue as a patient-safety and workforce-safety issue. It links long hours, heavy workload, inadequate staffing, and shiftwork with increased medical errors and calls for system-level strategies including appropriate staffing, realistic workloads, reasonable work hours, and contingency staffing plans. The item was reframed from a blanket legal claim about mandatory overtime to the supported fatigue/safety principle.
questions.source_name: American Nurses Association — Addressing Nurse Fatigue to Promote Health, Safety, and Well-Being for All
questions.source_detail: ANA Position Statement, effective May 27, 2026: fatigue is a nurse and patient safety crisis; long hours, workload and inadequate staffing are linked to errors; employers and nurses share mitigation responsibilities.

questions.stem: An adult has fever, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, focal crackles, and no obvious alternative diagnosis. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The findings raise concern for community-acquired pneumonia and warrant diagnostic evaluation, including chest imaging when clinically indicated.","B":"The findings establish allergic rhinitis without further evaluation.","C":"The findings prove bacterial pneumonia and identify the causative organism without imaging or microbiologic assessment.","D":"The findings are normal and require no clinical evaluation."}}
questions.rationale: Symptoms and focal lung findings can raise suspicion for community-acquired pneumonia, but clinical findings alone do not establish etiology. ATS/IDSA CAP guidance applies to adults with clinically suspected and radiographically confirmed pneumonia. The revised item therefore asks for suspicion and evaluation rather than claiming the symptom cluster alone confirms CAP.
questions.source_name: ATS/IDSA — Diagnosis and Treatment of Adults with Community-Acquired Pneumonia
questions.source_detail: Official ATS/IDSA guideline, published October 1, 2019 with additional resources updated through 2023; guideline management framework addresses clinically suspected and radiographically confirmed CAP.

questions.stem: A client has a cough lasting more than 3 weeks, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, and hemoptysis. What should the nurse do?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Recognize possible pulmonary tuberculosis, promptly escalate for TB evaluation, and initiate airborne infection-isolation precautions when presumptive infectious TB is being evaluated in healthcare.","B":"Treat the presentation as an uncomplicated common cold without further evaluation.","C":"Assume seasonal allergies despite the hemoptysis and systemic symptoms.","D":"Delay evaluation until the cough has persisted for several more months."}}
questions.rationale: CDC lists cough lasting 3 weeks or longer, hemoptysis, chest symptoms, unexplained weight loss, fever, and night sweats among pulmonary TB findings. Healthcare TB infection-control programs should ensure prompt detection and airborne infection-isolation precautions for confirmed or presumptive infectious TB disease.
questions.source_name: CDC — Clinical Overview and Signs/Symptoms of Tuberculosis Disease
questions.source_detail: CDC 2024-2025 clinical guidance: pulmonary TB symptoms include cough ≥3 weeks, hemoptysis, weight loss and night sweats; healthcare settings require prompt detection and airborne infection isolation for confirmed or presumptive infectious TB.

questions.stem: A client with a soft-tissue infection develops rapidly progressive swelling, severe pain out of proportion to visible skin findings, high fever, and hypotension. What is the priority interpretation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Suspect necrotizing fasciitis and obtain immediate surgical evaluation; imaging should not delay surgical exploration when suspicion is high.","B":"Assume uncomplicated cellulitis and delay escalation until oral antibiotics have been completed.","C":"Treat the findings as a benign allergic rash because severe pain is expected with allergy.","D":"Wait for skin necrosis to become extensive before considering a deep soft-tissue infection."}}
questions.rationale: CDC describes pain out of proportion to local skin findings, rapid progression, systemic toxicity, bullae or necrosis as warning features of necrotizing fasciitis. It is a surgical emergency; imaging can assist in selected cases but should never delay surgical exploration when clinical suspicion is high.
questions.source_name: CDC — Clinical Guidance for Type II Necrotizing Fasciitis
questions.source_detail: Current CDC guidance: pain out of proportion, rapid progression and systemic findings heighten suspicion; imaging should never delay surgical exploration; prompt surgical management is essential.

questions.stem: A client develops unilateral calf swelling, warmth, and tenderness after prolonged travel. Which diagnostic approach is most appropriate when lower-extremity DVT is suspected?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use a validated pretest-probability assessment and, according to that probability, evaluate with D-dimer and/or proximal or whole-leg ultrasonography.","B":"Diagnose DVT from symptoms alone without objective testing.","C":"Use a positive D-dimer alone to establish DVT in every patient.","D":"Rule out DVT solely because the client can walk without severe pain."}}
questions.rationale: ASH diagnostic guidelines use validated pretest probability to guide DVT testing. Low-probability patients can begin with a highly sensitive D-dimer followed by ultrasound when needed, while intermediate- or high-probability patients commonly require proximal or whole-leg ultrasonography. A positive D-dimer alone does not diagnose DVT. The prior item was corrected from the oversimplified instruction to obtain a 'Doppler ultrasound' based only on symptoms.
questions.source_name: American Society of Hematology — Guidelines for Diagnosis of Venous Thromboembolism
questions.source_detail: ASH 2018 VTE diagnosis guideline, reviewed by ASH in 2022 and retained for ongoing monitoring: lower-extremity DVT recommendations 5-8 use pretest probability with D-dimer and proximal/whole-leg ultrasonography; positive D-dimer alone is not diagnostic.
